newsitem.title: CANADA: Saudi suspect said refusing to cooperate with FBI.
newsitem.headline: Saudi suspect said refusing to cooperate with FBI.

text.p: A suspect wanted in the truck bombing in Saudi Arabia that killed 19 U.S. servicemen last year has dismissed his lawyer and said he does not want to cooperate with U.S. authorities, the lawyer said on Thursday.
"He said, 'No deal, no cooperation,' and that was it," lawyer Doug Baum told Reuters. "If he gets rid of me, then there's no way for this deal to go ahead. He's burned his bridges."

The suspect, Hani Abdel-Rahim Hussein al-Sayegh, was charged in Canadian court documents as the driver of a car that gave the go-ahead signal for the bomb-laden truck involved in the attack last year on Khobar Towers.

U.S. officials have long sought to question Sayegh about the June attack on the compound that housed U.S. military personnel in Dhahran in eastern Saudi Arabia. The bombing killed 19 Americans and injured hundreds.
Canada issued a conditional deportation order against Sayegh on May 14 but has not stipulated where he should go.

The leading candidates are Saudi Arabia or the United States, but if he refuses to give evidence on who was behind the attack it raises the question as to whether Washington will want him unless it has an iron-clad case for convicting him.

Baum said Sayegh, who had said he did not want to go to Saudi Arabia for fear of his life, had until May 29 to make such a representation to Citizenship and Immigration Minister Lucienne Robillard but did not do so.
U.S. officials in Washington had expressed cautious optimism on Thursday that Sayegh would be sent to the United States soon.

"It does look promising that he will be brought to the United States," said one official familiar with the delicate discussions involving Sayegh. "We are closer to some sort of an agreement. Progress is being made."

U.S. officials said the problem had been reaching a firm agreement with Sayegh. Among the issues to be resolved were his legal status when brought to the United States and what considerations, if any, he might receive if he cooperated.

"They are very fragile discussions. They have gone back and forth for some time. He's very wishy-washy," one official said. "He keeps changing his mind" on whether he will cooperate and what he will receive in return.
Among issues to be resolved, officials said it still had to be decided whether Sayegh would be brought to the United States as a witness, a subject of the investigation or a suspect.

One official described it as a difficult decision for Sayegh. "He is in a a foreign country. He is wondering, 'What will happen to me? What will happen to my family? Am I doing the right thing?' He may never see his homeland again."
Baum said Sayegh's decision to let him go was in a meeting Friday and they had another meeting on Monday to try to wrap up their affairs.

Another Saudi apparently mistakenly linked by Canadian authorities to the Khobar bombing, Fahad al-Shehri, was flown back to Saudi Arabia on Thursday, Baum said. Saudi Deputy Interior Minister Prince Ahmed bin Abdul-Aziz was quoted in March as saying that Shehri was not wanted in any case.

Shehri, who had been held in the same Ottawa prison as Sayegh, was charged at a Canadian refugee hearing with being a terrorist but the Canadian government official presenting the case told reporters he was not linked to the bombing.

Baum said Shehri had sought to be sent to Britain, where he had last lived, but Britain refused to have him. Baum said he had proposed other destinations but they were deemed unacceptable either by Canada or by the countries themselves.
